name: Giant Omphalocele

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Imaging Diagnostic Criteria for Giant Omphalocele

criteria.description: Presence of a large midline abdominal wall defect at the base of the umbilical cord
Herniation of abdominal viscera including liver and intestines into a membranous sac
Presence of a translucent sac covering the herniated organs
Prenatal or postnatal imaging confirming size and contents of the omphalocele
Identification of associated congenital anomalies (e.g., cardiac defects)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of a large midline abdominal wall defect with herniation of abdominal organs covered by a membranous sac confirmed clinically or by imaging
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical and supported by prenatal ultrasound or postnatal imaging.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Large midline abdominal wall defect with herniated viscera
searchTerms: midline abdominal hernia with organs outside

pathognomonic.symptomName: Presence of a translucent membranous sac covering herniated organs

common.symptomName: Respiratory distress secondary to pulmonary hypoplasia
searchTerms: respiratory distress due to lung underdevelopment
poor lung function causing breathing problems
problems with sucking or swallowing in infancy
failure to gain weight as baby

occasional.symptomName: Pulmonary hypoplasia leading to chronic lung disease
searchTerms: underdeveloped lungs causing chronic lung disease
lung hypoplasia leading to breathing issues
chronic respiratory problems from small lungs
hernia at belly button after surgery

occasional.symptomName: Developmental delay secondary to associated anomalies
searchTerms: delayed development due to other anomalies
scar tissue inside abdomen after surgery

rare.symptomName: Sepsis due to sac rupture or infection
searchTerms: blood infection due to sac infection
kidney defects linked to abdominal wall defect
coagulation issues due to liver disease
blood clotting disorder related to liver

laboratory: Elevated liver enzymes if hepatic involvement
Coagulation profile abnormalities in liver dysfunction
Infection markers if sac rupture occurs
imaging: Prenatal ultrasound showing abdominal wall defect with herniated organs
Postnatal abdominal X-ray and ultrasound confirming omphalocele size and contents
genetic: No specific gene identified; may be associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 13, 18
Genetic testing recommended to rule out syndromic associations
other: Physical examination revealing large abdominal wall defect with membranous sac

distinguishingFeatures: Defect is usually right of umbilicus without covering sac
Smaller defect with intact abdominal wall fascia
No herniation of liver or large viscera

redFlags: Sac rupture leading to risk of infection and sepsis
Severe pulmonary hypoplasia causing respiratory failure
Presence of multiple associated congenital anomalies
references: Moore KL, Persaud TVN. The Developing Human: Clinically Oriented Embryology. 11th Edition. Elsevier; 2019.
